title: Metric collection and querying
description: Collect metrics from a large fleet and return either one node's metric history or a metric aggregated across all nodes. Support metric discovery, one-year retention, and fast recent queries.
focus: durable collection, time-series storage, fleet pre-aggregation, availability, freshness, and multi-datacenter operation.

children.value: Collect metrics from hundreds of thousands of hosts, expose one-minute time series, and serve both node-level and fleet-wide queries without scanning the fleet on every request.

This guide now follows the expanded collection-and-querying prompt. Fleet aggregation and metric discovery are base functionality. Alerting is a follow-up. Examples and proposed policies are explicitly labeled.
The progression, not just the final boxes
Collect observations → query one node → query a fleet aggregate → discover a node's metrics → fix read amplification, freshness, storage, and partition behavior.

threshold alerts, week-over-week differences, moving averages/min/max/p99, multi-colo architecture, 10×/100× growth, and a ten-year extension. Multi-colo hosts are part of the context; start with one colo to explain the core and then extend it explicitly.
This differs from the earlier small-fleet variant

The base is no longer “hundreds of hosts plus graphing and alerting.” It is a much larger, availability-first query platform. The walkthrough must earn fast fleet queries, a node-metric catalog, and the specified SLOs before spending time on alert delivery.
Hundreds of thousands of hosts; hundreds of metrics each
Many millions of node-metric series. Capacity must include series state, not just event bytes.
Normalize observations into one-minute chart buckets; raw emission cadence is not the output resolution.
Tens of thousands of read QPS
Bound the work of each query and size read CPU, storage, and response bandwidth. Fleet reads must not enumerate all hosts at request time.
One-minute reporting; lower granularity allowed after one month
Retain minute-level history for at least the recent month. Coarser old data must have explicit resolution semantics.
One year of retention; arbitrary intervals within it
Support both recent and historical range queries, including ranges crossing tier boundaries. Do not support only a few fixed “last hour/day” answers.
Emit provisional open-minute results; waiting for a minute to close plus a lateness buffer can violate this target.
P99 <100ms for recent data: last 24 hours
The fast tier must cover the full recent 24-hour window, not just the last hour.
Multiple seconds acceptable for older data
Permit colder storage, wider scans, and coarser rollups while still returning the full requested range.
At least 99.99% availability; availability over consistency
Prefer usable local/stale/partial results and independently available intake over globally coordinated fresh answers during partitions. State durability and completeness limitations.
Node and metric strings average 32 characters; value is a double
Budget names, timestamps, and framing, then explain dictionary encoding rather than counting only the 8-byte value.
Metric discovery for a given node
A queryable, retained node-to-metric association index with liveness/history semantics.
Clarifications that still change the design
Which fleet aggregation: sum, average, or something else?
Support sum/average appropriate to the metric. For CPU percentage, use an equal-node average of per-node minute averages unless capacity-weighting is requested.
What does a missing or silent node mean?
Unknown, not zero. Return reporting-node count and coverage; an expected-node count from the catalog is timestamped and may itself be stale.
How much temporary data loss risk is acceptable while remaining writable?
Base ACK promises a durable local copy, not a global majority. Replication is asynchronous and producer replay is bounded. A stronger replica-ack policy is an explicit availability trade-off.
How long can observations arrive late or be replayed?
Use a bounded automatic-repair horizon, for example 24 hours, and a smaller normal lateness allowance. Older recovery uses an explicit backfill path.
Where is read latency measured in a multi-colo deployment?
At a serving colo with the relevant recent data/materializations. Geographic network delay is separate; global low latency requires appropriate hot-data placement.
Are sparse metrics common? Are names/units globally compatible?
Catalog metric kind and unit, reject or separate incompatible definitions, and choose materialization based on fan-out and read load.

the sub-minute freshness SLO cannot hold for observations trapped behind an arbitrarily long network outage. The service should stay useful, expose staleness/coverage, and repair later. Do not claim complete, current fleet answers while a colo is disconnected.

Define availability, freshness, completeness, and durability as separate SLIs. 99.99% is about 52.56 minutes/year of full-outage time as an illustration, not a guarantee obtained merely by drawing three replicas. An unusable empty response must not be counted as success to manufacture four nines.
Build the answer in front of the interviewer
Requirements → entities → interfaces → working baseline → targeted deep dives → final design.
As in the Top-K reference, expose a limitation before introducing the component that fixes it. Here, fleet aggregation and sub-minute visibility are central, not optional optimizations.
Illustrative 45-minute plan; the document is a reference, not a script to recite in full.
Both query forms, discovery, minute granularity, freshness, availability, and hot/cold latency targets.
Active series, ingest rate, fleet query amplification, and hot-data size.
Observation/bucket/catalog identities; node, fleet, discovery, and ingest contracts.
Collect, read one series, combine a fleet series, and list a node's metrics. Mark the bottlenecks.
Hot storage + hierarchical pre-aggregation; availability/freshness + replay-safe updates. Use interviewer probes to choose depth.
Multi-colo and one of alerts, 10×/100× growth, or ten-year history.
Map mechanisms to SLOs and disclose the remaining trade-offs.

Meet all six axes and exceed at least two, including depth or fault tolerance. Strong signals here are identifying the fleet-query explosion unprompted, separating sample/node/time weighting, publishing open buckets correctly, and admitting what AP behavior cannot guarantee during partitions.
Do not spend the deep-dive time on email retries before the base query system meets its contract. Do not replace reasoning with a list of database and streaming product names.
The scale makes fleet pre-aggregation necessary
300,000 hosts, 200 metrics per host, six observations per metric per minute, and 30,000 reads/s
. These values are within the supplied ranges, not additional fixed requirements. Units below are decimal.
Batched host requests, at one flush per 10 seconds = 30,000/second
Naive tuple = timestamp 8 + node 32 + metric 32 + value 8 = 80 bytes
Naive observation payload = 480 MB/second, before framing and replication
A 24-byte compact-reference model = 144 MB/second, before its extra metadata

The 80-byte model assumes identifier characters encode to one byte on average. A compact model uses scoped dictionary references rather than repeating names; producer IDs, revisions, dictionaries, and protocol headers still cost space. Numeric dictionary IDs are not automatically portable across colos.
Why the second query changes the architecture
One node, one metric, last 24h = 1,440 minute points
One widespread fleet metric, naive read = 300,000 × 1,440
The desired fleet response is still only 1,440 points.

That is the decisive reason to materialize dense fleet aggregates. Reading hundreds of millions of contributions for every request is not compatible with tens of thousands of read QPS and P99 under 100ms.
Provisional updates are additional work; this does not reduce all processing to one million operations/s.
Cumulative summaries simplify aggregation/replay but do not automatically reduce network bytes. They may be larger than compact raw observations.
Recent hour, 48 bytes per published bucket
Even the RAM-oriented working set is a distributed budget, before indexes and object overhead.
Plan the entire recent SSD tier. Three total copies would be 12.4416 TB before overhead.
Even pre-aggregated reads need significant egress. JSON/metadata can increase this.

For comparison, use a 48-byte logical published bucket: series reference, bucket time, aggregation sum, aggregation weight/count, min, and max. Raw sample coverage, revisions, canonical source fragments, sketches, indexes, and replication bookkeeping are
. The sum/count semantics depend on the series, as described later.
This is not an all-in hardware recommendation. Add live canonical/repair state, log retention, compaction space, metadata, fleet materializations, and headroom. Three copies
across three colos would not have the same cost as three copies total.

These calculations also assume a stable 60M-series population. Ephemeral hosts, changing metric names, and labels can make the number of distinct series retained over a year much greater than the simultaneous active count.
Keep event identity, aggregation identity, and time distinct
Stable instance identity, display name, colo, authenticated source identity, and lifecycle. Do not silently join a reused hostname to an unrelated old machine.
Canonical name/namespace, unit, kind (gauge/counter/distribution), and aggregation policy. Incompatible units must not enter the same fleet series.
, plus transport identity such as producer epoch and sequence for retries.
, monotonically increasing source revision, and cumulative sufficient statistics for that producer's observations.
One published node/metric/minute value, coverage, and a materialization revision/frontier.
Metric, minute, logical aggregation partition, current contributions, reporting-node count, and revision. FleetMinute is the final chart series, not a list of node series.
Node-to-metric association, definitions, first/last seen information, active/history status, and retention bounds.
Time is already in the prompt:

preserve the host's observation timestamp. Add ingestion/processing timestamps to measure lag; do not replace event time with collector arrival time. Otherwise a replayed observation from an outage looks current.

Use UTC bucket boundaries and clock synchronization; use monotonic clocks for local elapsed-time scheduling. Validate implausible timestamps and expose clock skew. Source revisions order versions of the same contribution; wall-clock last-write-wins is not a substitute.
A 10-second observation cadence cannot detect every shorter spike. Durability of captured observations and fidelity of the sampling process are different guarantees.

There is one active metric agent/exporter per node. Restart epochs identify disjoint observation fragments; retries preserve the original epoch, revision, timestamp, and payload. If overlapping producers are allowed, define deduplication of their observations explicitly rather than counting both as independent contributions.
Both chart queries and discovery are first-class

GET /v1/nodes/host-17/metrics/cpu.utilization/series
    ?from=2026-09-14T08:00:00Z
    &to=2026-09-15T08:00:00Z
    &step=1m
    &timeAggregation=avg

Response: one time series
  node, metric, unit
  points: [{ time, value, coverage, provisional }]
  resolution_segments
  data_watermarks
  completeness
Query the metric across the fleet

GET /v1/metrics/cpu.utilization/series
    ?scope=fleet
    &aggregation=avg
    &from=2026-09-14T08:00:00Z
    &to=2026-09-15T08:00:00Z
    &step=1m

Response: one aggregated time series
  metric, unit, aggregation_semantics
  points: [{ time, value, nodes_reported, coverage, provisional }]
  resolution_segments
  data_watermarks
  completeness
The client does not supply hundreds of thousands of node IDs.
is a distinct query path. At the base one-minute resolution, a recent 24-hour request returns up to 1,440 points for either query form.

GET /v1/nodes/host-17/metrics?view=retained&cursor=...

Response:
  metrics: [{ name, unit, kind, first_seen, last_seen, available_from }]
  catalog_as_of
  next_cursor

view=active   -> recently reported metrics under a documented liveness policy
view=retained -> metrics with retained history, including inactive ones
Ingest without making hosts database clients

The authenticated node must match the publishing identity; do not accept arbitrary source impersonation. The example shows the observation form. The worked aggregation path has the agent normalize those observations and send cumulative minute fragments in this second format:
Fragments are versioned replacements, not deltas to add on every delivery. If accepting raw observations directly, deduplicate their stable
identities before deriving fragments. A 202 is acceptance into durable intake, not a claim of complete fleet publication.

Crossing a resolution boundary must return explicit resolution segments or an agreed coarser output step; never truncate a year-long query and imply it is complete. Sub-minute exact answers are outside a one-minute reporting contract.
Build the four behaviors before optimizing them

props.aria-label: A node agent sends timestamped observations to a collector, which persists them

children.value: Start with one logical collection path and a timestamped store. Explain the durability acknowledgment rather than putting an undocumented in-memory queue between receipt and success.
one collector cannot handle the stated fleet; a sole durable copy is vulnerable to disk loss; the system needs replication, bounded buffers, and partition behavior.

props.aria-label: A graph client asks a node-series service to read the matching range from the observation store

children.value: Read the requested observations, group them into UTC minute buckets, and return one time series. Order/index data by series and time rather than scanning unrelated nodes.
repeated raw-to-minute aggregation, cold random I/O, and unbounded historical scans will not meet the new QPS/latency targets.

props.aria-label: A naive fleet query identifies reporting nodes and merges their minute values into one series

children.value: This naive implementation establishes the semantics: for each minute, combine values from reporting nodes, using the chosen weighting, and expose coverage.
432 million input contributions for one widespread metric's 24-hour query. Explicitly reject this as the final serving path; we will precompute the fleet series.

props.aria-label: Ingestion updates a node-metric catalog, and discovery queries read that catalog

children.value: Record node-metric associations and serve discovery from an index. Do not discover names by scanning a year's observations.
writing catalog presence on every sample would create millions of unnecessary metadata updates/s; the catalog must also remain useful during metadata outages.

We can now trace collection, both query forms, and discovery. The next changes are earned: distributed intake, availability-first replication, indexed hot storage, minute materialization, hierarchical fleet aggregation, and a low-write-rate catalog.
Choose an acknowledgment contract compatible with the AP goal
Host-local batching/spooling, natural onboarding, and failover to another reachable collector.
Authentication, backpressure, retry storms, and identifying silence versus network failure.
Central cadence control and clear failed-scrape signals; simple exporters.
Requires discovery and scrape ownership. A consistent configuration service can coordinate schedules, but collectors need cached assignments if it fails.
An agent reads OS/application metrics locally and pushes remotely, isolating credentials and networking from application threads.
Agent lifecycle and collection overhead need monitoring.

Clients should not hold broad database credentials or manage database partitions. A durable queue/log is a valid ingestion boundary, either behind the frontend or through tightly scoped producers. A queue name does not define its acknowledgment, partition, or replay guarantees.
The agent gives observations or summary revisions stable identities and keeps a bounded durable spool.
Any reachable authorized collector can append to its persistent intake log. Grouped fsync may amortize cost; acknowledge only the durably persisted prefix.
stored on the receiving collector's durable disk
. It does not wait for a cluster-wide or cross-colo majority.
Replicate asynchronously toward a target of multiple copies on independent failure domains. Replication progress and publication progress are separately observable.
Where the agent protocol supports it, retain replay data until replication confirmation, not merely local acceptance. Spool age/bytes remain bounded and exhaustion is explicit.

A local-disk ACK survives a collector process restart with its disk intact. If that disk is permanently lost before another copy exists, recovery depends on the producer spool; loss is possible if neither copy remains. This is an explicit trade-off, not zero-loss replication.

If the interviewer requires every accepted write to survive immediate loss of its receiving node without producer assistance, wait for another durable replica or a quorum. Then explain which network partitions prevent success. Do not silently promise both unconditional write availability and synchronous multi-replica durability.
A durable broker is an alternative, not a loophole

A locally replicated Kafka-style log can provide a stronger within-colo acknowledgment while independent colos continue through cross-colo partitions. That can be a good practical choice. Its local quorum still limits progress when that quorum is lost. State the partition scope instead of calling every quorum-based subsystem “fully AP.”

Place routing/configuration outside the per-observation critical path. Cache valid discovery and authentication material. New node-metric associations can be registered asynchronously; unknown compact IDs can fall back to canonical identities rather than make an ID allocator a global ingest dependency.
Use logical ingestion partitions and batch-friendly source affinity, then route per-node materialization by node/series identity. Split fleet aggregation by
, not by metric name alone. Physical ownership can move without changing logical contribution identities.

Retries may duplicate accepted data. Correct aggregation relies on stable source identities and replacement/version semantics, not an unsupported exactly-once transport claim. A full spool, full disk, or unbounded partition requires a surfaced limitation; no success-shaped silent drops.
Explain the storage layout that makes range queries cheap

A TSDB is a reasonable implementation, but the answer is the data layout and execution path beneath its label. Both base query forms should become a small number of sequential reads of an already-materialized series.

NodeMinute:
  partition key: (view_id, node_id, metric_id, UTC_day)
  clustering / sort key: minute_start
  fields: value, coverage, revision, provisional, aggregation statistics

FleetMinute:
  partition key: (view_id, metric_id, aggregation_kind, UTC_day)
  clustering / sort key: minute_start
  fields: value, nodes_reported, coverage, revision, provisional

SeriesArchive:
  partition key: (view_id, scope, series_id, resolution, time_partition)
  clustering / sort key: bucket_start
  fields: aggregation_sum, aggregation_weight, extrema, coverage
  example: day partitions for minutes; month partitions for hours

SourceContribution (canonical processing / repair state):
  key: (node_id, producer_epoch, metric_id, minute_start)
  value: highest source revision and its cumulative statistics

NodeMetricCatalog:
  partition key: node_id
  clustering / sort key: metric_name
  fields: definition, first_seen, last_seen, retained-history bounds

A 24-hour interval crosses at most two UTC-day partitions for a single series. Avoid an unbounded partition containing a metric's full fleet and full history. Fleet partials and their processing state are separate from the compact final FleetMinute query rows.

identifies a serving-colo/materialization generation. Queries choose one advertised view; independently computed colo outputs must not overwrite each other using unrelated local offsets or wall-clock timestamps. Replicate canonical contributions and rebuild each view from them while those inputs are retained.

If the backend cannot merge a source fragment by logical revision safely, append immutable revision-keyed records and select the highest known source revision during materialization. Do not assume ordinary wall-clock last-write-wins implements this rule. Derived output publication needs checkpoint/version discipline so a stale worker cannot overwrite a newer view.
What the storage engine is doing
Append ingest/revision records sequentially for durability and recovery; batch writes rather than issuing a disk seek for every sample.
Maintain recent indexed state in memory, keyed by series and minute, including open-minute revisions.
Flush sorted, time-bounded chunks/blocks and keep a sparse series/time index so a query locates relevant blocks directly.
Compress regular timestamps with deltas or implicit positions, and values with an appropriate numeric encoding such as XOR/delta schemes where beneficial.
Compact revisions and generate coarser archives under explicit replacement/checkpoint rules. Expire whole time blocks when safe instead of deleting billions of individual points.

Use a practical number of packed shard files, not one open file per each of 60 million series. Indexes, memory allocation, decompression CPU, and compaction I/O can dominate long before nominal disk capacity runs out.
The hot tier covers 24 hours, not just one hour
Open buckets and approximately last hour
One-minute values, rapid revisions, low-latency recent reads. RAM is not the only durable copy.
Indexed SSD/flash storage, with read replicas and memory caching where useful.
One-minute node and fleet series. This is the fast path for the P99 <100ms target.
Cheaper SSD/HDD or another warm tier with efficient sequential access.
Still one-minute history; multiple-second queries are acceptable.
Older than one month through one year
Cold compressed blocks/HDD/object storage with an index.
Hourly or another agreed lower resolution; no silent claim of minute-level historical precision.

Hot copies and caches are placement choices over the retained dataset; do not accidentally count every tier as disjoint new data unless it really is duplicated. If raw observations are needed for alerting or backfill, budget their bounded log separately. Before canonical input expires, make the required archive/checkpoint copies durable under the chosen policy; historical materializations are not disposable once their rebuild inputs are gone.

Use fixed-retention archives: one-minute data for 30 days, hourly data for a year, with overlapping hourly summaries if convenient. This is the useful RRD principle: bounded slots per admitted series at each resolution, not necessarily a literal RRD file for each metric.

Define the population being averaged. A node-minute value may average raw observations; a fleet-minute value may average node-minute values; an hourly chart point may average valid published minute values. Carry the sum and weight/count of
population. Do not confuse raw sample count, reporting-node count, and valid-minute count.
For example, when hourly chart values represent the mean of published minute values, store
. Raw-sample-weighted or time-weighted means need their own sufficient statistics. Coverage and optional raw extrema are additional data, not interchangeable counts.

The query planner divides a request into non-overlapping retained segments, or uses an agreed uniform coarser step. It must not double-count the overlapping minute/hour archives. Return actual resolutions and boundary/coverage semantics. An arbitrary range endpoint does not imply exact sub-minute reconstruction from minute buckets.

A full year at one-minute resolution contains 525,600 values: about 4.2MB for doubles alone, before timestamps and framing. Old-data downsampling and efficient block reads are therefore relevant even to a single node's query.
Series/time indexes, compression, retention, and rollups are native concerns.
Its actual replication/availability model, hot-data layout, cardinality limits, and aggregation semantics.
Series/day partitioning plus time clustering gives efficient bounded ranges.
Ordering is within the relevant partition/key layout, not a promise that every NoSQL database globally sorts all keys. Avoid hot or unbounded partitions.
Can implement the schema with partitions and batch writes; useful for metadata too.
At this scale, index/write/retention overhead and operational sharding may be less attractive. SQL does not inherently mean “CA” under CAP.
Packed blocks and a simple index can exploit the narrow query model.
Higher development cost and responsibility for durability, repair, availability, indexing, and safe evolution. Reuse established storage primitives where possible.
Precompute along time and across nodes
reduces the number of points for long intervals.
reduces the number of node series read for each metric. They solve different amplification problems; doing only one is insufficient.
First make the fleet value unambiguous
fleet_avg(metric, minute) = sum(node_value for reporting nodes)

, not an average of every raw observation. If one node reports six observations averaging 100 and another reports one observation of 0, the equal-node average is 50; the raw-sample average is about 85.7. Either can be meaningful, but the API must say which it returns.

For capacity-weighted CPU or memory percentage, carry the agreed node weights and use weighted sums. For additive metrics, sum node values/rates where the units permit it. Missing nodes are excluded with coverage reported, not converted to zero.

props.aria-label: Source revisions produce canonical node-minute values, which feed partitioned fleet partials and a final fleet series

children.value: Normalize each node's observations into minute sufficient statistics and a published node-minute value.
Assign each node to exactly one logical partial partition for a metric, for example
. This prevents one popular metric from funneling every update into one worker.
Each partial tracks current node contributions and emits its sum, reporting-node count, coverage, and revision periodically.
A final combiner consumes the current version of each disjoint partial and writes the small FleetMinute series.
Fleet reads fetch that series from the hot/cold query store, just like node reads. They do not fan out across the original hosts.
With 200 widespread metric names and 256 partials per metric, emitting partials every five seconds yields about
into final combiners, spread by metric. This is an illustration, not a fixed partition count; distinct metric-name cardinality may be far larger than 200.
One concrete retry-safe protocol has the local agent maintain a cumulative summary for
. Each emission has a higher source revision and includes all observations in that fragment so far. A receiving materializer retains the highest known revision for that fragment.

Fragment F, revision 1: sample_sum=40,  sample_count=1
Fragment F, revision 2: sample_sum=110, sample_count=2

After receiving revision 2:
    replace F's revision 1 contribution
    canonical F is (110, 2), not (150, 3)

Retry revision 2: no extra contribution
Late revision 1: no rollback
Different payload with the same revision: surface a producer/protocol error

Restart fragments are combined only if their observations are disjoint. This source-snapshot protocol is an internal extension to the raw tuple interface, not a claim that raw tuples carry these statistics already. An alternative is deduplicating stable raw event IDs before deriving snapshots, with the corresponding state/replay cost.

When a node's minute value changes, replace its old contribution in the partial. For a sum/average, update the numerator by the value delta; increment the reporting-node count only on the node's first valid contribution. At the next level, replace the previous partial snapshot rather than adding every emitted partial.

Apply the same principle to temporal rollups: a revised minute is a replacement contribution to its hour, not another minute. Min/max may need a versioned multiset, a suitable index, or recomputation when an old extremum is replaced; subtraction alone does not maintain them.
Do not merge overlapping replica totals

Two colos can hold overlapping observations. Adding their locally computed fleet totals double-counts the overlap. Reconcile canonical source fragments by identity and revision, then aggregate disjoint node partitions. Replicas of the same logical partial are alternative views of that partial, not additional nodes to sum.
Materialize selectively, without leaving the SLO to chance

Dense or heavily queried metrics should be pre-aggregated. A metric reported by one node can reuse that node's series; a small sparse membership may use a bounded parallel merge. The metric-to-node membership index determines fan-out without scanning observations.

Set the on-demand fan-out threshold from the recent-read SLO and promote before it becomes too expensive, leaving room for backfill/catch-up. Do not promise P99 <100ms for an unbounded cold fallback. During promotion, publish a new materialization only after it covers the advertised interval/frontier.
Logical partial IDs remain stable when physical workers move. If changing the partition plan, use a versioned cutover and never sum both old-plan and new-plan partials.
One-minute buckets do not mean one-minute publication delays
An observation at the start of a minute cannot wait until that minute ends
wait through processing and late-arrival buffering while still meeting a strict sub-minute visibility objective. Publish the open bucket repeatedly.
Emit updated node and fleet values every few seconds. Mark them provisional and expose their input frontier/coverage.
Continue accepting normally late observations without delaying the already-visible result.
Mark the bucket settled under the policy. This does not prove every expected machine reported.
Replace the affected source/minute contributions, repair hour/day rollups, and invalidate/update cached revisions.
Use an explicit validated backfill/rebuild or reject/quarantine with clear status. Never blindly increment expired aggregates.
Transport + local durable intake: budget 5 seconds
Cache staleness allowance: at most 5 seconds
Total budget: 40 seconds, leaving 20 seconds of headroom

These are design budgets to validate under the stated workload, not measured product benchmarks. Measure from observation emission to visibility in each base query path. Batch/stream lag, not just RPC latency, belongs in the freshness SLO.
Open-minute node/fleet results and hot query state.
Always-on state and processing cost, checkpoint/replay complexity, and incremental-correction semantics.
Historical compaction, hour/day rollups, backfills, reconciliation, and repair.
Often simpler/cheaper for bulk work, but a long scheduled interval alone cannot satisfy visibility <1 minute.
Streaming serves freshness; batch verifies/rebuilds historical materializations from retained canonical input.
Share aggregation definitions and version outputs so the two paths do not silently compute different values.

Flink/Spark or custom partitioned consumers can implement this. Explain their input partitions, local state, checkpoint recovery, output identities, and lag policy. The framework name does not establish end-to-end exactly-once results, especially across asynchronous colos and external stores.

Keep canonical contribution/version state for the supported replay/repair horizon. An old replica returning beyond that horizon must resnapshot/rebuild, not reintroduce stale contributions whose deduplication history has expired.
List metric names without scanning metric history
as an explicit association index. Ingestion observes or the agent registers a new association; the discovery API reads the node's bounded, paginated metric list.
Insert on first observation/definition change and refresh liveness in batches. Do not issue a metadata update for every one of six million observations/s.
Expose both recently reporting metrics and metrics with retained data. Keep associations until their historical data expires, even after a node disappears.
Replicate/cache catalog data and return its as-of time. An ingest path should not wait on a global catalog quorum for every metric.
A reverse index supports sparse fleet queries and materialization planning. Batch membership changes and distinguish live membership from historical presence.
Track metric kind/unit/namespace. Surface incompatible definitions rather than average percentages with bytes or unrelated counters.
Authenticate publishers and authorize node/metric discovery and queries. Catalog visibility should not bypass data access controls.

At 60 million associations, catalog/index memory is real work, but still far smaller than a per-observation index. Returning an approximate expected-node count is acceptable only if it is labeled with its liveness policy and freshness; it is not proof of fleet completeness.

A stale catalog must not fabricate a definitive “metric never existed” result if a data lookup could legitimately find newly arrived history. Define unknown/not-yet-discovered versus an empty requested time range explicitly.
Protect the recent read path from fleet size

Both hot query forms read a small published series. Route to an available hot replica, fetch indexed sequential blocks, merge any current open bucket, and return values plus coverage. Avoid fleet fan-out, full raw scans, and synchronous control-plane calls.
An end-to-end budget, not a cache slogan

These are allocation targets, not a claim that summing component P99s proves the service P99. Measure actual end-to-end tails under realistic node/fleet query mixes, output size, compaction, and failures. Older ranges use a separate multi-second budget and read concurrency pool.
When caching helps, and when it does not

Indexed hot storage already makes individual ranges cheap, and changing open buckets limit cache lifetime. A generic cache is not the primary solution. Cache popular fleet results, immutable historical ranges, catalog pages, and decompressed blocks when reuse justifies it.

For fresh results, use short TTLs or revision-aware invalidation within the visibility budget. Include metric, scope, aggregation/weighting, interval, resolution, and relevant materialization version in the key. Prevent cache stampedes; do not let a stale cache conceal a delayed publisher.
Host batching, compact identities, grouped fsync, horizontal ingestion partitions, and backpressure.
Partition state, use compact representations, bound active windows/repair horizons, and avoid per-series files or heavyweight objects.
Shard partials by node identity; emit bounded-frequency partial snapshots; distribute final combiners by metric.
Popular fleet query / hot read shard
Read replicas, result/block caching, coalescing identical requests, and independent query-node scaling.
Separate foreground reads, ingestion, compaction, historical scans, and backfill budgets. More stateless query servers alone do not add disk bandwidth.
Jitter reconnects, prioritize current data, rate-limit replay, and reserve replication/repair bandwidth.
Efficient encoding/compression and justified coarser historical resolution; never secretly omit part of the requested interval.
Answer “how much can one component handle?” honestly
Use a measured capacity at the target payload/SLO, not a generic product QPS number. For example,

a collector sustains 100K observations/s and is operated at 60% of that rate, 6M observations/s needs 100 collectors before extra failure-domain constraints. This is a conditional sizing example, not a benchmark claim.

a query replica sustains 2K representative requests/s within the tail target and we operate at 60%, 30K reads/s needs 25 replicas before failover/headroom adjustments. Check bytes/s, CPU, and backend capacity as well.
600M observations/s; 6B series. Federate ingestion/storage cells, control cardinality, distribute state, and budget network/repair explicitly.
3M QPS. Scale serving/replicas/egress and cache reused fleet series; keep each query independent of raw fleet fan-out.
More/larger partial partitions; final output still minute series.
Add hierarchical cell/colo aggregation, but only combine disjoint canonical contributions. Do not create one global counter/lock.
Approximately linear growth before compression/retention changes.
More cells and lifecycle management, tiering, and admission policy. Downsampling helps time volume, not unbounded identity growth.
Return useful information without pretending it is complete
Restart supervised agents, replay durable spool, and show gaps/no-data status.
Uncaptured observations cannot be recreated. Lost host disk may remove replay data not yet replicated elsewhere.
Spool, retry reachable collectors with the same identities, use backoff/jitter, and catch up under a bandwidth budget.
Freshness is impossible while no route exists. Spool exhaustion must be surfaced, not hidden.
Fail over intake; recover its durable local log if disk survives. Replays merge idempotently.
A local ACK was not an in-memory receipt, but also was not a majority-copy guarantee.
Recover from any asynchronous replica or producer replay still retained.
If neither exists, accepted data can be lost under the declared AP durability policy. Stronger acknowledgments change the availability trade-off.
Restore checkpoint/canonical inputs, rebuild current contribution state, and publish a versioned replacement after catch-up.
Serve available prior materializations with lag/coverage; do not add replayed partial totals twice.
Use another available replica or a valid cached result. Isolate failed dependencies and bound retries.
Return an explicit error if no usable result exists; never turn a transport failure into zero-valued metrics.
A shard or colo is unreachable
Keep independent intake/serving available; expose partial or stale data and per-source/colo watermarks.
A global sum may be incomplete and an average biased toward reporting nodes. Do not label either a complete fresh fleet answer.
Use cached assignments/definitions, canonical identities, and asynchronous catalog updates.
New discovery may lag. Coordination-heavy placement changes can pause without blocking all established data paths.
Backlog, disk pressure, or compaction overload
Admission control, reserved headroom, bounded queues, tier expiration, and separate recovery budgets.
Finite resources cannot absorb unlimited outages; never delete required history or falsely acknowledge discarded data.
The most fragile part of this design
replicated inputs, revisable aggregate state, and global completeness claims

. A healthy collector can coexist with stale fleet materializations, duplicate contributions, or a hot final aggregator. End-to-end publication lag and aggregate correctness deserve first-class monitoring.

Measure oldest spool age, replication exposure, rejected/late records, queue lag, node/fleet publication age, coverage, catalog lag, hot-tier latency, and repair backlog. Keep a separate lightweight health path so a total monitoring outage is not expected to alert only through the same broken pipeline.

A local single-writer/checkpoint mechanism for a derived shard may use coordination; that is not a requirement for a global ingest quorum. During such a worker outage, intake and available query snapshots continue while the affected freshness/completeness degrades explicitly.
A concrete lost-ACK and replay sequence
An agent persists summary revision 7 and sends it to collector A.
A durably appends it but its response is lost; the agent retries the same revision at collector B.
Replicated canonical state identifies one fragment at revision 7. Neither node nor fleet counts increase twice.
Revision 8 later replaces revision 7, including any already-seen observations. It is not another independent sum.
If an old replica subsequently sends revision 6, it cannot roll the contribution back. A replica beyond the repair horizon must rebuild instead of rejoining with unbounded stale state.

Start with the single-colo pipeline above, then deploy independent intake, canonical-state processing, and serving in multiple colos. Replicate source identities/revisions and retained blocks asynchronously. Avoid a cross-colo quorum in the base ingest path.
Hosts can use reachable intake; local query endpoints remain available; no single active colo owns all ingestion.
Asynchronous views differ. Deduplicate failover/replayed contributions; budget replication and replicated hot data; expose coverage/watermarks.
Simpler normal ownership and serving model; fewer simultaneously active processing copies.
Promotion and catch-up delay, possible asynchronous replication loss window, and a traffic hotspot. A disconnected passive cannot provide the active's newest observations.
How an active-active fleet result converges
Stable canonical node/metric/producer identities are shared across colos; local dictionary IDs are translated in transport rather than assumed globally equal.
Two receivers may accept the same source fragment. Reconcile that fragment using the highest source revision, not by adding the receivers' copies.
Each serving colo builds its view from the canonical node contributions it currently knows, using the same disjoint logical aggregation partitions.
Within that view, combine one current snapshot per logical partial. Do not add overlapping whole-colo fleet totals.
When connectivity returns, source revisions converge and dependent minute/hour values are corrected through the same replacement protocol.

Replicating source contributions is more expensive than shipping only a few fleet totals, but avoids double-counting overlapping failover traffic. If using geographically disjoint aggregation instead, enforce and explain an exclusive contribution-home/ownership protocol; do not merely assume colos never overlap.

For a truly local sub-100ms query on any node's recent data, that serving location needs the relevant hot replica or a latency-compatible route. A compact global fleet series is cheap to replicate; tens of millions of node series are not. Choose serving regions and replication placement deliberately and include the cost in capacity.

During a cross-colo partition, available endpoints return their known state and freshness/coverage metadata. The system does not promise a globally complete answer within 60 seconds when inputs cannot cross the partition. Complete consistency and partition-time availability cannot both be asserted by changing a database label.

Control-plane updates, catalog definitions, and optional alert ownership need their own conflict/availability policies. Keep them out of every observation's critical path where possible. The base chart API is eventually consistent; strict single-owner notification delivery is an optional separate concern.
Clarify retention versus durability before multiplying disks

“Extend durability to ten years” could mean keeping ten years of queryable history, keeping the same history safer for longer, or both. Ask which resolutions and historical query latencies must remain available.
Preserve hourly data for ten years
Ten times the hourly archive buckets: about 252.288 TB unreplicated for a stable 60M-series population under the 48-byte model, before the recent minute tier and overhead.
Minute for one month; hour for one year; day for ten years
A proposed lower-cost policy. A full overlapping ten-year daily archive is about 10.512 TB unreplicated at the same fixed series population, but daily data cannot answer hourly historical questions.
Independent failure-domain copies, checksums/scrubbing, backup and catalog durability, media migration, restore exercises, and retention of required encryption keys and schema definitions.

Use cold compressed/object storage and a durable series/time manifest, with retrieval latency stated explicitly. Incrementally roll up rather than repeatedly scan the full decade. Preserve the sufficient statistics or sketches required by supported historical computations.

The fixed-population arithmetic is only a floor. Ten years of ephemeral nodes and metric churn can dominate cardinality. Retire expired metadata carefully, preserve historical identity, and distinguish logical delete/retention policies from immediate removal of every backup copy.
One available pipeline, two fast chart paths, one catalog

use the blue paths to explain each query, the green paths to explain how its data is produced, and the amber path to discuss availability and replication. Schemas and partition keys sit beside the stores they belong to.
The numbered boxes are discussion anchors. Names such as Redis are illustrative choices, not additional requirements.
Metrics collection and querying: annotated interview whiteboard

Read APIs feed a query planner, optional cache, hot node and fleet time-series tables, historical archives, and a discovery catalog. The write path sends authenticated observations from agents to a local durable intake log, then canonical node-minute workers and partitioned fleet aggregation. The diagram labels API paths, record identities, schema partition and sort keys, hot and cold retention, freshness targets, and asynchronous replication. Numbered boxes and R/W labels provide a single-picture interview walkthrough.
METRICS: ONE PICTURE TO EXPLAIN THE SYSTEM
Auth, rate limits, serving view / colo
Choose node, fleet, catalog or archive
Read one stored series, not the entire fleet
R3: discover names without scanning data
Minute fragments are cumulative, not deltas
Replace old input; never add retries
1,440 rows/day; read at most 2 day partitions for 24h
Latest hour RAM; full recent 24h on SSD; read replicas
Replicate hot views; cache only when query reuse helps
Discovery reads an index, not history
1m to 30d; 1h to 1yr; older reads take seconds
Packed compressed blocks; HDD / object storage
Batch repair and compaction replace revised inputs
Expire inputs only after required archive durability
Walk: R1 node / R2 fleet / R3 discovery / R4 history, then W1-W5, then the ACK and replication boundary.
7 and 8 are logical tables, not mandatory separate clusters. A TSDB or wide-column backend must implement the shown access and merge semantics.

Use the record layouts, sharding keys, and R/W labels as prompts for the explanation. The optional cache does not carry durability or correctness; canonical revisions and the declared availability policy do.
Availability-first metric collection with node, fleet, and discovery query paths

Node agents batch timestamped observations and revisioned minute summaries. Reachable collectors acknowledge durable local intake and replicate asynchronously. Canonical node-minute processing feeds hot and cold node-series storage, partitioned fleet aggregation, and a node-metric catalog. Fleet partials produce a materialized fleet series. Query services read the node or fleet series and discovery reads the catalog. The same pattern can run in multiple colos with asynchronous canonical-input reconciliation and explicit coverage metadata.
Latest source revision per fragment; one node contribution per minute
Replace, do not re-add; coverage, checkpoints, and bounded repair
Combine one version of each partial
One node series OR one fleet series; node metric listing
Actual resolution, provisional values, coverage, and freshness watermarks
Optional alert processors consume appropriate raw/summary inputs; they are not required for the base query path.
Each box is logical and independently partitionable. In multi-colo operation, reconcile canonical source contributions before deriving fleet views; do not add overlapping replicated fleet totals.
Capture the observation with its source timestamp and stable producer identity; batch and spool at the host.
Persist at a reachable collector, return the declared local-durability receipt, and replicate asynchronously.
Merge source revisions into canonical node-minute state and publish open-minute node values.
Update the association catalog on new/changed metadata, not once per raw observation.
Feed disjoint fleet partials, replace older partial revisions, and publish FleetMinute values frequently enough for the visibility SLO.
Serve node/fleet recent queries from indexed hot materializations; use coarser/cold archives for older ranges.
Checkpoint, compact, expire, and repair under bounded horizons, preserving identity/version semantics and exposing gaps.

Queries remain available from usable local materializations during many failures, while coverage/freshness can degrade. No component is allowed to turn missing regions into zero values or a falsely complete fleet result.
Add advanced behavior without changing the base story
Threshold alerts and avoiding spurious notifications

Run rule evaluation outside the collector's intake handler. Use appropriate raw observations or extrema for threshold detection: a minute average can hide a brief observed breach. If the base transport exports only summary statistics, enable a raw/event stream for relevant rules or retain the required timing information at the agent.

Define immediate versus sustained thresholds, hysteresis, cooldown, and no-data behavior. Raw extrema do not by themselves reconstruct the exact duration of a breach. For a fleet rule, require suitable coverage; a missing colo must not look like a genuine drop in utilization.

Use a durable alert state machine, stable activation IDs, one fenced owner per alert key where needed, and an atomic state/notification-outbox update. Replayed input must not create a second logical activation. Ownership coordination may temporarily pause alerts without blocking the base AP ingestion/query service.

Notification workers retry with a stable delivery ID. One logical activation does not guarantee exactly-once email: a crash after provider acceptance but before recording success can duplicate delivery unless the provider supports idempotency.
, or completed calendar weeks in a named timezone. Do not compare an incomplete current week with a complete previous week accidentally.
For a positive previous average, fire when

, subject to coverage and rule duration. Define behavior for zero/negative baselines. Use the declared population's sum/weight statistics; weekly fleet averages of minute fleet values are not automatically raw-sample-weighted node averages.
Schedule this long-window computation appropriately and use retained rollups. Do not scan two weeks of raw fleet observations on every arriving sample.

Moving averages use bounded window sums/weights or compatible time buckets. Min/max can merge retained extrema, with explicit handling of replaced/expired contributions. Partial coarse bucket boundaries need finer input or a disclosed approximation.

For p99, define the population first: node observations, fleet observations, or request latencies are different. Percentiles are not additive; averaging host or bucket p99s does not give a global p99. Use underlying observations or compatible mergeable histograms/quantile sketches, such as KLL with an agreed error bound.

Versioned cumulative sketches must replace older versions of the same contribution before merging across disjoint contributors. Otherwise replay can double-count a distribution. Historical p99 requires retaining sketches in historical tiers; mean/min/max alone cannot reconstruct it. Budget their storage separately.
Gauge means, counter rates, and time weighting

A gauge's sample average is not necessarily its time-weighted average under irregular sampling. A time-weighted mean needs value-duration contributions and a coverage/interpolation policy; do not hold the last observation through an unbounded gap.

A cumulative counter requires reset-aware deltas/rates before interpreting a minute value. Process restart or counter reset must not become a negative event rate. Fleet sums of rates and averages of percentages have different semantics.

Cache metric handles after registration, avoid repeated name/label allocation, and keep network/disk work off application threads. Use striped/thread-local counters and compatible local histograms where appropriate, then merge at the exporter. Atomic gauge snapshots are useful, but arbitrary thread-local gauges should not be summed without semantic justification.

Do not hold a global metrics lock during serialization or I/O. Prefer cumulative counters to read-and-reset races, bound queues/cardinality, and accept a slightly non-atomic telemetry snapshot when that is preferable to hurting the monitored application's request path.
What if exact raw history is required for the whole year?

The base minute/coarse archives do not preserve every observation. Retain compressed raw blocks separately, index them by canonical series/time, and budget replication, repair, retrieval, and long-range query cost. Do not satisfy an exact raw query with a lossy rollup and claim equivalence.
What if a replay arrives after canonical state has expired?

Finite automatic-repair windows need a defined boundary. Reject/quarantine the late update explicitly or run a controlled backfill from sufficient authoritative data, publishing replacement materializations. An old replica must resnapshot rather than merge stale fragments whose version/deduplication protection is gone.
Why not partition every stage by metric name?

Common metrics would concentrate hundreds of thousands of sources on one ingestion/aggregation partition. Keep node/series affinity for source state and shard fleet partials by a disjoint node hash. Only the small final series needs a metric-centric serving key, where read replicas and selective caching address popularity.
Can a consistent metadata service coexist with an AP data path?

Yes, for tasks such as placement or scrape scheduling, provided every observation/query does not synchronously depend on it. Cache established assignments, let independently available intake persist canonical identities, and pause only operations requiring new coordinated decisions. Explain the exact degraded behavior rather than assigning one CAP label to every component.
What you can say while drawing
These are short transitions, not a monologue. Pause for interviewer probes and adjust the assumptions they challenge.

“The base system collects timestamped observations and returns either one node's metric series or one metric aggregated across the fleet. I also need a node-to-metric discovery API. I will clarify the aggregation's weighting and missing-node semantics, and leave alerting as a follow-up.”

“For an example, 300,000 hosts times 200 metrics gives 60 million series. At six observations per minute, that is six million observations per second. A naive 24-hour fleet query for one common metric reads 432 million contributions to return just 1,440 points. That makes pre-aggregation a primary design requirement.”

“I will first connect agents, durable intake, and a series/time store. A query service reads one node's range. Then I will add a naive fleet merge to establish its semantics and a catalog to list a node's metrics. That completes functionality, but the fleet merge and raw scans cannot meet the SLOs.”

“I would materialize minute series, partition by series and time bucket, and store each range sequentially. Recent buffers live in memory and the full last 24 hours are on indexed flash, not only the last hour. Older data can move to cheaper storage, with hourly rollups after a month and explicit output resolution.”

“For a fleet average I first compute a value per node per minute, then combine disjoint node partitions into a FleetMinute series. Equal-node averaging is different from averaging all raw samples. I would partition a common metric's aggregation by node hash so it does not create one hot worker.”

“One-minute resolution does not mean waiting more than a minute to publish. I would publish provisional open-minute values every few seconds and correct them later. Each revised contribution replaces its older version; it is not an additional sum. Streaming serves freshness and batch processing handles historical repair and compaction.”

“I would not gate all intake on a global quorum. The base acknowledgment is a durable local append, followed by asynchronous replication and bounded producer replay. That has a stated loss window if all unreplicated copies disappear. If we require synchronous replica durability, I would call out the partitions where writes stop rather than still claiming unconditional availability.”

“Each colo can ingest and serve its known materializations. We replicate canonical source contributions and reconcile their identities/revisions; we must not add overlapping whole-colo totals. During a partition I would expose stale or partial coverage, not pretend a global result is complete and fresh.”

“Both chart queries read compact materialized time series, discovery uses a separate association index, and the hot tier covers the 24-hour latency target. Minute publication and historical rollups are distinct. The conscious trade-offs are AP staleness/completeness, the local-ACK durability boundary, and reduced old-data resolution. I would size and monitor the complete publication and query paths, not just collector RPCs.”

Discover all metrics for a node
Catalog API, retained/active semantics, and low-write-rate association indexes

Tens of thousands of read QPS

RAM/flash placement for the full hot interval

One-year retention; older data can be coarser
80-byte naive tuple, compact-ID alternatives, and excluded overhead
TSDB internals / solution without a TSDB
Logs, memory state, ordered chunks, compression, indexes, and backend trade-offs
Hybrid serving/repair design and output consistency
Selective caching, freshness limits, node-hash partials, and read replicas
Faults, network outages, and fragile components
Recovery paths, loss limits, completeness, and end-to-end monitoring
Explicit growth table, formulas, and non-benchmark sizing examples
Resolution/cost choices, identity churn, and long-term preservation
Placement, asynchronous convergence, and no overlapping-total addition
Dedicated follow-ups, including coverage, weighting, sketches, and notification idempotency
How this aims above the Senior bar
Both query forms and discovery are explicit; weighting, outage scope, and latency measurement are clarified.
The answer reaches published node/fleet series and catalog output, not merely an ingestion queue.
Explains local durability versus quorum availability, precompute versus sparse fan-out, hot/cold storage, and stream/batch costs.
Handles replayed revisions, loss windows, stale global views, failed processors, and repair beyond retained state.
Identifies fleet read amplification and hot aggregation keys; sizes series state, egress, retention, and growth.
Distinguishes sample/node/time weighting, replaces cumulative contributions correctly, publishes open buckets, and explains the storage layout.
Falls short in three or more axes, cannot start despite hints, or makes too many incorrect assumptions.
Falls short in one or more axes; cannot reach, or leaves no time for, follow-ups.
Meets all axes, completes the solution with level-appropriate hints, explains alternatives, and handles one or two follow-ups.
Meets all axes and exceeds at least two, including depth or fault tolerance.
Completes with minimal hints and handles several follow-ups.
Meets all axes and exceeds four or more, with novel insights or solutions beyond expectations.
No document guarantees a rating. Demonstrate why the components fit, respond constructively to hints, and avoid occupying the whole interview with one detailed mechanism.
Technical shortcuts in the notes that should not be repeated literally
CAP is about the consistency/availability trade-off during a partition, not the query language. Explain the actual replication/read/write protocol.
useful range ordering depends on partition and clustering/sort-key design. A hash-partitioned key alone does not make all data globally ordered.
useful, but the stated fast-read target covers 24 hours, so the rest of that interval also needs a credible flash/indexed path.
true with the appropriate cadence and workload, but a slow batch-only publisher cannot meet visibility under one minute.
Can you defend the full expanded prompt?
I state both time-series query forms and make node-metric discovery a base requirement.
I distinguish supplied SLOs from assumptions about weighting, missing nodes, repair horizons, and failure domains.
I can derive 60M series, 6M observations/s, and the 432M-to-1,440 fleet-query reduction for the example.
I budget identifier bytes, provisional update work, read egress, hot storage, retention, and replication separately.
I first build collection, node queries, naive fleet queries, and discovery, then explain why each optimization is needed.
I explain push/pull, host buffering, local durable acceptance, asynchronous replication, and the resulting loss window.
I preserve event time and stable producer identity through retries, restarts, and multi-colo failover.
I can draw the series/day/time schema, explain TSDB mechanics, and cover the full last 24h with a fast storage path.
I distinguish sample-weighted, node-weighted, and temporal means, and never treat missing nodes as zero.
I replace cumulative source/partial revisions instead of adding them repeatedly, including during hour/day rollups.
I publish provisional minute buckets frequently enough for the sub-minute visibility target.
I compare streaming, batch repair, and selective pre-aggregation for dense versus sparse metrics.
I handle hot aggregation keys and read shards, and can reason about component capacity and 10x/100x growth.
I explain active-active/active-passive colos without summing overlapping replica totals or promising fresh completeness during partitions.
I can extend retention/durability to ten years and explain alerting, comparisons, and percentile follow-ups with the right information.
I close against availability, freshness, query latency, discovery, retention, and honest degradation, leaving room for interviewer probes.

Capture with identity. Accept durably under an explicit availability policy. Publish minutes before they settle. Precompute the fleet, not every query. Read indexed hot series. Expose coverage. Repair by replacement, not double-counting.
approach you supplied: a working baseline, visible bottlenecks, and justified evolution. The monitoring architecture is specific to this prompt, not a reuse of Top-K's restricted query windows.

One self-contained guide, no external runtime libraries. This is one defensible architecture, not the only acceptable answer.
